# Mūlapariyāya Sutta (MN 1 (PTS MN i 1))

**ID:** MN 1 (PTS MN i 1)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Root of All Things

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mūlapariyāya Sutta* ("The Root of All Things" or "The Discourse on the Root of Existence") is the opening discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya* (MN 1) [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 1980]. In this foundational text, the Buddha investigates the cognitive processes through which the notion of a permanent self emerges from perception, expounding how craving, conceit, and views govern distortion [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 1980]. The discourse examines a sequence of phenomena extending from the physical elements (such as earth, *pathavī*) to cosmological planes and ultimate categories; an uninstructed person perceives a phenomenon and "conceives" (*maññati*) it in terms of selfhood—conceiving himself as it, in it, apart from it, or conceiving it as "mine" [Buddhist Philosophy 2012a; Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 1980]. In contrast, disciples in higher training and arahants experience the same range of phenomena directly without conceptual proliferation or attachment [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003].

Due to its conciseness and enigmatic phrasing, the text has traditionally been considered one of the most profound discourses in the Pali Canon [Bodhi 1980]. It is interpreted at length in the commentary *Papañcasūdanī* and its associated subcommentary (*ṭīkā*) [Bodhi 1980]. Major modern English translations include those by I. B. Horner, Bhikkhu Bodhi (both independently and in collaboration with Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli), Bhikkhu Sujato, and Suddhāso Bhikkhu [SuttaCentral; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. Bhikkhu Bodhi published a comprehensive study and translation of the sutta along with its commentarial apparatus under the title *The Discourse on the Root of Existence* [Bodhi 1980; Bodhi 2003].

Curated parallels recorded for the sutta include Chinese translations preserved in the *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 106), the *Ekottarika Āgama* (EĀ 44.6), and the individual translation *Lèxiǎng jīng* (樂想經, T 56); the sutta is also cited in the Theravāda *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 9.2, *Amatārammaṇakathā*) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus computational analysis confirms significant alignment with T 56 and the *Ekottarika Āgama* (T 125), as well as cross-language matches in Sanskrit and Tibetan texts such as the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, *Lokaprajñapti*, and *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* [DharmaNexus]. Internally within the Pali Canon, DharmaNexus identifies heavy text reuse with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa-aṭṭhakathā*, the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa-ṭīkā*, and related suttas including the *Brahmanimantanika Sutta* (MN 49) and *Chabbisodhana Sutta* (MN 112) [DharmaNexus].
